query: Consider a TaVCrW refractory high-entropy alloy. The objective is to calculate its melting temperature and related thermodynamic properties using Density Functional Theory (DFT). The standard approach (TOR-TILD) relies on expensive thermodynamic integration. We hypothesize that substituting the reference potential (EAM) with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) and replacing thermodynamic integration with free energy perturbation (FEP) can achieve significant speedups while maintaining sub-meV accuracy, provided the MTP accurately reproduces the ab initio phase-space distribution even for complex liquids. Prior work suggests that electronic excitations (specifically the gap in the Density of States at the Fermi level) can shift the melting point by tens of Kelvin, and that Short-Range Order (SRO) in the solid phase can introduce a stabilization energy of ~2-3 meV/atom. However, there are limitations: (1) The empirical 'underbinding/overbinding' rules for GGA-PBE/LDA functionals do not hold for V and Cr at 0K, potentially propagating errors; (2) High-temperature magnetic fluctuations are typically neglected but may be relevant. The computational cost must be reduced by >80% compared to the baseline TOR-TILD method. Propose the specific structural mediator (the MTP's ability to reproduce phase-space distributions) that enables the substitution of TI with FEP. What is the boundary condition regarding the supercell size and temperature range (2000-2400 K) needed to validate the SRO contribution? Design a falsification experiment comparing the new method against the original TOR-TILD on a benchmark system (e.g., a simpler alloy) to ensure the free energy difference does not exceed 0.5 meV/atom.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the EAM potential with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) trained on DFT data for TaVCrW, and replacing Thermodynamic Integration (TI) with Free Energy Perturbation (FEP), will reduce computational cost by >80% while maintaining sub-meV accuracy in melting temperature prediction. This is enabled by the MTP's ability to accurately reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, particularly capturing the electronic excitation effects (Fermi level gap shifts) and Short-Range Order (SRO) stabilization energy (~2-3 meV/atom) in the liquid and solid phases.
generation.material_initial_state: TaVCrW refractory high-entropy alloy, equiatomic composition, in both solid (BCC) and liquid states.
generation.intervention: Develop a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) trained on DFT data for TaVCrW. Replace the standard TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration with Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) calculations. Include corrections for electronic excitations and magnetic fluctuations (LSF) in the potential training or post-processing.
generation.conditions: Temperature range 2000-2400 K (covering the expected melting point). Supercell size must be sufficient to capture SRO (e.g., > 200 atoms) to validate the ~2-3 meV/atom stabilization energy. Pressure: 0 GPa (ambient).
generation.structural_mediator: The MTP's fidelity in reproducing the DFT phase-space distribution, specifically the ability to model the local atomic environments and electronic density of states (DOS) near the Fermi level, which governs the electronic excitation contribution to the free energy and the SRO stabilization.
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles: The MTP approximates the DFT potential energy surface with high fidelity, allowing for efficient sampling of the phase space. FEP calculates the free energy difference between the solid and liquid states by perturbing the system between states, avoiding the slow convergence of TI. The accuracy depends on the MTP's ability to capture the specific electronic structure (gap shifts) and magnetic fluctuations (relevant for Cr) which contribute to the free energy landscape. The SRO stabilization energy (~2-3 meV/atom) arises from local chemical ordering in the liquid/solid interface, which the MTP must reproduce to avoid errors in the melting point prediction.
generation.predicted_outcome: The melting temperature of TaVCrW will be calculated with an uncertainty of < 10 K (sub-meV accuracy in free energy). The computational cost will be reduced by >80% compared to TOR-TILD. The predicted melting point will be in the range of 2100-2300 K (typical for Ta-based RHEAs), with a stabilization energy contribution from SRO of ~2-3 meV/atom.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD method using EAM potentials and thermodynamic integration, which is computationally expensive and may suffer from inaccuracies in electronic excitation and magnetic fluctuation modeling for V/Cr.
generation.boundary: The method is valid only if the MTP is trained on a diverse set of configurations including liquid, solid, and high-temperature magnetic states. The supercell size must be large enough (>200 atoms) to capture the correlation length of SRO. The temperature range 2000-2400 K must be sufficient to observe the phase transition. The method may fail if the 'underbinding/overbinding' errors for V and Cr at 0K propagate significantly into the high-temperature regime.
generation.uncertainty: High uncertainty regarding the accuracy of the MTP in capturing the specific electronic excitation effects (gap shifts) and magnetic fluctuations for the TaVCrW system, as no direct transferable data exists for this specific alloy. The 'underbinding/overbinding' rules for V/Cr at 0K may introduce systematic errors in the free energy calculation. The exact magnitude of SRO stabilization energy in TaVCrW is assumed to be similar to other RHEAs but requires validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a benchmark calculation on a simpler, well-characterized refractory alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW) using both the new MTP+FEP method and the baseline TOR-TILD method. Ensure the MTP is trained on DFT data for NbMoTaW.
measurements: Melting temperature (Tm) calculated by both methods
Free energy difference (ΔF) between solid and liquid phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The new method is falsified if the free energy difference (ΔF) between the solid and liquid phases calculated by MTP+FEP deviates from the TOR-TILD result by more than 0.5 meV/atom at the melting point, or if the predicted Tm differs by more than 20 K. Additionally, if the computational time reduction is less than 80%, the hypothesis is falsified.

The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

The finite-temperature properties were derived from the free energy F α ( α represents the fcc or hcp phase) by accounting for lattice expansion and LSFs at finite temperature, which is expressed as F α ( w , T ) = E int ( w , { M I }) − TS mag

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. On the other hand, these alloys are brittle at room temperature, leading to significant limitations of their application as structural materials. La

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
